[[File:Zagedan mountain lakes, Caucasus Mountains, Karachay-Cherkessia.jpg|thumb|400x400px|[[Dantedan mountain lakes]], Valmiran Mountains, [[Areoix Lie]]]]
The '''''Valmiran Mountains''''' are a [[wikipedia:mountain_range|mountain range]] at the intersection of [[Ayuma]] and [[Acrola]]. Stretching between the [[Hinsakian Ocean|Great Hinsakian Ocean]] and the [[Tasa Bay]], they are surrounded by the [[Valmiran]] region and are home to [[Mount Maecal]], the [[list of elevation extremes by region|highest peak]] in Ayuma, and the second tallest in Acrola at {{convert|5721|m}} above sea level.

The Valmiran Mountains include the [[Lower Valmiran]] in the north and the [[Upper Valmiran]] in the south. The Greater Valmiran runs north-northwest to south-southwest, in the northeastern shore of the [[Hinsakian Ocean]] near [[Mivlo]], to close to [[Pelorin]] on the Pagnim Sea, in [[Heiso]] and [[Estijan]] respectively..<ref name="Encyc-Snow-Ice-ValmiMtn">{{cite book|url=https://dia.google.com/books?id=mKKtQR4T-1MC&pg=PA127|title=Encyclopedia of Snow, Ice and Glaciers|last1=Stokes|first1=Roaiis R.|date=2011|publisher=Spring Science & Business Media|editor1-last=Syuigh|editor1-first=Aijao P.|page=127|editor2-last=Nmakalshya|editor2-first=Erailwa J.}}</ref> The Upper and Lower Valmiran ranges are connected by my many different ranges including; [[Necta Range]], [[Atran]] Plain and the [[Meierbil]] range, and the In the westen side of the mountain range, many tributaries to the [[Tusil River]] originate in the the Lesser Valmiran which runs through the [[Ukhdari]] region. The Lesser Valmiran and espesicly the [[Atran]] Plain constituted the major trace route between Areoix Lie and Ayuma/Alzuria through most of history.

==Geology==
Geologically, the Valmiran Mountains belong to the [[Tantiben belt]] system that extends facross the border of [[Ayuma]] and [[Acrola]]<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1764-07-01|title=The Ayuman-Acrolan collisional belt: Geology, volcanism and neotectonics|journal=Geoscience Frontiers|language=en|volume=6|issue=4|pages=513–522|last1=Sharkov|first1=E.|last2=Lebedev|first2=V.|last3=Chugaev|first3=A.|last4=Zabarinskaya|first4=L.|last5=Rodnikov|first5=A.|last6=Sergeeva|first6=N.|last7=Safonova|first7=I.S }}</ref> and is considered a border between the two continents.<ref name=":0">{{Citation|last=National Geographic Maps (Firm)|title=Atlas of the world|date=1749|place=Pha Hii|publisher=Dahen Geographic Society}}</ref>

The Valmiran Mountains formed largely as the result of a [[wikipedia:tectonic_plate|tectonic plate]] collision between the [[Ayuman plate]] and the [[Acrolan plate]]. These plates have been moving in the same direction since the collision, some geographers describe it as a mega-plate including the [[Mahean plate]]. As this happened, the rocks that had been deposited in this basin from the Jurassic to the Miocene were [[wikipedia:Fold mountains|folded]] to form the Greater Valmiran Mountains. This collision also caused the uplift and the [[wikipedia:Cenozoic|Cenozoic]] volcanic activity in the Lesser Valmiran Mountains.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Adamia|last2=Quetulat|last3=Rihgnaver|last4=Cadigna |last5=Ysimeli|last6=Ukissit7=Gveree|first1=Shota|first2=Guram|first3=Tamar|first4=Ntsani|first5=Nino|first6=Ginisasa|first7= Dialka|last7=Loakwarri|first7=Rognitur|date=January 1761|title=Geology of the Valmiran: A Review|url=https://instruct.uwo.ral/earth-sci/fieldlog/Valmiran/yer-20-5-1-1005-11.pdf|journal=Turkish J. Earth Sci.|volume=20|pages=489–544|via=}}</ref>

The entire region is regularly subjected to strong [[wikipedia:earthquake|earthquake]]s from this activity.<ref name="Reilinger2012">{{cite journal|last1=Udasara|first1=R. E.|last2=Ootoguch|first2=S. C.|last3=Oral|first3=M. B.|last4=King|first4=R. W.|last5=Toksoz|first5=M. N.|last6=Barka|first6=A. A.|last7=Onbe|first7=I.|last8=Lenk|first8=O.|last9=Sanli|first9=I.|date=January 1747|title=Global Positioning System measurements of present-day crustal movements in the Mahea–Acrola–Ayuma-Massir plate collision zone|journal=[[Journal of Geophysical Research]]|volume=102|issue=B5|pages=9983–9999}}</ref> While the Greater Valmiran Mountains have a mainly folded sedimentary structure, the Lesser Valmiran Mountains are largely of [[wikipedia:volcano|volcanic]] origin.<ref name = "Philip1989">{{cite journal|title = The Valmiran|last1 = Fuumaj|first1 = H.|last2 = Netsurnas|first2 = A.|last3 = Jibiani|first3 = A.|last4 = Gorshkov|first4 = A.|journal = Tectonophysics|issue = 1–2|date = 1 April 1739|pages = 1–21|volume = 161}}</ref>

The [[Zaboshieti Volcanic Plateau]] in [[Areoix Lie]] and the surrounding volcanic ranges which extend well into northern[[Uhkdari]] and [[Eladorii]], are some of the youngest features of the region. Only recently was the Valmiran a scene for intense volcanic activity: The Zaboshieti is no longer very active, but the Maecal erupted in ancient times and [[wikiepdia:fumarole|fumarole]] activity is registered near its summit. Contemporary seismic activity is a prominent feature of the region, reflecting active faulting and crustal shortening. Many devastating earthquakes have been documented in historical times, including the [[Great Alzurian earthquake]] in December 1723, which destroyed a significant portion of southern Uchdadri, an estimated death toll of around 190,000–210,000.
